column4: The command not to drive away those who call on God morning and evening stages a direct rejection of the socially lowly; 6:53 explains that people are tested through one another and asks whether these are the ones God favored.

This ayah uses the section’s root ب ل و for people being tested by one another, then voices the status question “Are these whom God favored?”; it directly exposes the same false reading of provision that the section corrects.
The ayah asks guardians to imagine leaving weak children behind in the context of orphan property; 4:10 names the consequence of consuming that property, making the orphan’s vulnerability familial.

The ayah details nursing a child, the father’s duty to provide and clothe, and the parents’ shared decision about weaning; it makes the section’s image of a child raised and sustained through care concrete.
After 76:8 depicts feeding the orphan, poor, and captive, this ayah says the feeders seek no repayment or thanks; it makes care an act toward the vulnerable rather than a claim to honor.
This ayah names feeding during severe hunger; 90:15 specifies an orphan of near kin, so the cited detail places material care inside the section’s family image.
The ayah calls wealth and children worldly adornment but says lasting good deeds are better; it sets the section’s perceived signs of honor against durable conduct.
The ayah names mutual boasting and competition in increasing wealth and children as features of worldly life; this directly parallels the section’s mistaken use of abundance as rank.
The command not to be impressed by a people’s wealth and children directly reverses the section’s claim that abundance proves a person honored.
This ayah repeats the command not to be impressed by wealth and children; its repeated reversal reinforces the section’s warning against treating visible provision as rank.
The ayah forbids killing children for fear of poverty and says God provides for both parent and child; it makes scarcity a boundary against withholding care from a child.
This ayah identifies the blind man who came in the scene begun by 80:1; it gives a concrete vulnerable petitioner whose arrival is met with neglect.
The ayah uses the section’s root ب ل و for testing and names loss of wealth among its trials; it gives a specific form of constriction that the section says should not be read as humiliation.
The ayah says people will be tested in wealth and selves; it reinforces the section’s account of material fortune as a trial, while its own context adds injury and hardship.

The ayah says God expands or restricts provision for whom He wills and places the keys of heaven and earth under His authority; it repeats the section’s root ق د ر while grounding provision in divine rule.

The ayah says one does not attain birr until giving from what one loves; the section’s dictionary branch for ي ت م says the orphan is neglected in his birr, and this ayah makes that goodness depend on costly giving.

The ayah distinguishes those who spent before victory from those who spent later while promising good to both; it gives a concrete Quranic scene for the section’s dictionary image of outdoing another in generosity.
The command to remain with those who call on God and not turn one’s gaze away toward worldly adornment draws a specific boundary against preferring visible status over humble people.
Following the command not to oppress the orphan in 93:9, this ayah says not to rebuff the asker; it extends the section’s care ethic to another vulnerable petitioner.
This ayah identifies the poor person in the same feeding passage as 90:14 and 90:15; it extends that passage’s concrete care from the near-relative orphan to a destitute person.
The ayah opens with turning away; 80:2 identifies the arriving blind man, making this a specific scene of the neglect the section’s dictionary note associates with the orphan.
This ayah introduces the person who considers himself self-sufficient; 80:6 shows attention being directed to him, a specific social-status contrast to neglecting the orphan.
This ayah shows the speaker devoting attention to the self-sufficient man introduced in 80:5; 80:8 and 80:10 describe attention diverted from the striver, exposing status-based regard.
This ayah introduces the person who comes striving; 80:10 says attention is diverted from him, a concrete parallel to the section’s neglected orphan.
This ayah says the striver of 80:8 comes in fear of God; 80:10 then describes turning away from him, sharpening the contrast between moral worth and received attention.
This ayah says attention is diverted from the striving petitioner introduced in 80:8; it completes the scene of overlooking the vulnerable while attending to the self-sufficient man in 80:5 and 80:6.
